<description>
{
 "summary": "Restricts descriptor expansion in DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::TopUpWithDB() to begin at range_start rather than index 0 for descriptors with a non-zero range start. In both TopUpWithDB() and Load(), sets m_max_cached_index directly to the derived index rather than incrementing from an initial value of -1.",
 "problem": "Importing a descriptor with range [N, M] derives and watches all keys from index 0 to M because top-up begins from m_max_cached_index + 1 (which starts at 0). This makes imports take O(M) time instead of O(M - N), temporarily treats scriptPubKeys below N as owned until the wallet is reopened (causing rescanned transactions below N to drop out of wallet balance upon reload), allows pathological range starts near 2^31 to stall the node, and causes redundant re-derivations on reload because m_max_cached_index was tracking a count instead of the actual derived index.",
 "evidence": [
  "Author benchmark: 'Importing wpkh(xpub/0/*) with \"range\": [600000, 600009] into a blank watch-only wallet goes from 19.5s to 0.09s on this machine.'",
  "PR description notes that Load() only expands [range_start, range_end), creating a discrepancy where keys below range_start are IsMine during import rescan but no longer IsMine after restarting the wallet."
 ],

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
